contribution.value: Releases OpenMiniSafety, a 1,067-question human-curated safety dataset, and benchmarks 66 quantized variants of 4 LLMs across four PTQ and two QAT methods, showing both PTQ and QAT can degrade safety alignment.

ev.quote: we introduce Open-MiniSafety, a human-curated safety dataset with 1,067 challenging questions to rigorously evaluate model behavior. We publicly release human safety evaluations for four LLMs (both quantized and full-precision), totaling 4,268 annotated question-answer pairs
This process yielded OpenSafetyMini - a refined dataset of 1,067 English prompts.
One of the previous open-questions benchmarks XSAFETY (Wang et al., 2023a) was consisted of two existing benchmarks and translated them into multiple languages.
We use SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2023), a multiple-choice benchmark, to assess a model's understanding of safety concepts rather than its refusal behavior.
We utilize the factual Question Answering multihop dataset HotPotQA (Yang et al., 2018) to evaluate LLM trustworthiness and reliability in mitigating hallucinations.

data_size.value: OpenSafetyMini: 1,067 prompts; 4,268 unique human-labeled question-answer pairs (over 20,000 human evaluations across five experts and four models).

ev.quote: Each expert evaluated 1,067 samples per model, including both quantized and non-quantized variants, see Table 2, resulting in a total of over 20,000 human evaluations, or 4,268 unique labeled question-answer pairs.

eval_metrics.value: Human safety rate (Safe / Unsafe / Error / Ambiguous)

ev.quote: Each model's response was classified into one of four categories: Unsafe, Safe, Error, or Ambiguous.
we employed the "LLM-as-a-Judge" approach using Gemma 2 27B (Team et al., 2024). Our results demonstrate a high 92% agreement with human judgments
Accuracy on a private test set serves as the evaluation metric.
AlignScore (Zha et al., 2023) evaluates hallucinations by measuring the consistency between the generated response and its relevant context.
In-Accuracy assesses whether the model's response contains the correct answer (Ni et al., 2024a; Moskvoretskii et al., 2025).
The interrater agreement, measured using Krippendorff's α, yielded a score of 0.623.

key_results.value: Human eval on LLaMA-3.1-8B: FP16 90.59% safe vs Abliterated 58.67% safe; QUIK int4 90.75% safe (≈ FP16); QUIP# int2 drops to 78.81% safe with errors rising to 6.28%
QAT on LLaMA-3.1-8B at int2: STE collapses SafetyBench to 51.50% and HotPotQA in-accuracy to 0.390; QLoRA falls to 36.30% / 0.265 (vs FP16 73.90% / 0.684)
Qwen2.5-1.5B at int2 QUIP# collapses XSafety safety ratio from 85.96% (FP16) to 5.96% (-80 pts), and OpenSafetyMini from 83.13% to 8.35% (-74.78 pts)
QUIK int4 on LLaMA-3.1-8B SafetyBench reaches 74.60% (best, beating FP16 73.90%); QUIP# int4 drops to 63.30%; AQLM int2 holds 59.80% while QUIP# int2 collapses to 54.70%
QAT LLaMA-3.1-8B QLoRA int2 LLM-as-Judge safety ratio drops to 40.29% on XSafety (-53.46 pts) and 24.77% on OpenSafetyMini (-68.29 pts vs FP16 baseline)
LLM-as-a-Judge (Gemma-2-27B) reaches 92% agreement with human safety judgments across 4,268 labeled QA pairs

ev.quote: Our results demonstrate a high 92% agreement with human judgments, validating the reliability of our evaluation procedure.

By assessing 66 quantized variants of these models using four post-training quantization (PTO) and two quantization-aware training (QAT) methods across four safety benchmarks—including human-centric evaluations—we uncover critical safety-performance trade-offs.
We employ 4 modern PTQ Methods: AWQ ... QUIK ... AQLM ... QUIP# ... For QAT we follow the standard choice of methods: STE ... QLoRA

strengths.value: Releases OpenSafetyMini, a new human-curated 1,067-prompt safety benchmark with 4,268 labeled human evaluations of quantized models.

ev.section: Our contributions and findings are as follows:
ev.quote: We introduce OpenMiniSafety, a human-curated safety dataset with 1,067 questions to evaluate model safety.

strengths.value: Broad sweep: 66 quantized variants across 4 PTQ + 2 QAT methods, 5 modern LLMs, 3 bit widths, 4 benchmarks.

ev.quote: we evaluate 66 quantized models by applying 4 state-of-the-art PTQ methods to 5 modern LLMs across 3 precision levels, as well as 2 QAT methods applied to 1 model across 3 precision settings.

strengths.value: Demonstrates 92% agreement between Gemma-2-27B LLM-as-a-Judge and five linguistic experts (Krippendorff alpha 0.623).

ev.quote: Our results demonstrate a high 92% agreement with human judgments, validating the reliability of our evaluation procedure.

strengths.value: Includes an Abliterated baseline (refusal-direction removed) and shows multi-choice benchmarks fail to detect this loss of alignment.

ev.quote: in the case of LLaMA, the benchmark fails to detect severe degradation and inaccurately ranks the model as safe.

weaknesses.value: Dataset filtering depends on GPT-4o deflection score so some valuable low-deflection prompts may be excluded.

ev.quote: Our dataset filtering relies on the GPT-estimated deflection score, followed by human validation to remove incorrectly marked unsafe questions.

weaknesses.value: QAT evaluation is limited to a single model (LLaMA-3.1-8B); QAT generalisation across architectures is not tested.

ev.quote: For QAT we focus on LLaMA 3.1 8B, following previous studies (Zhelnin et al., 2024).

weaknesses.value: Authors acknowledge focus is on PTQ; deeper QAT investigation is left to future work.

ev.quote: Our evaluation currently focuses on post-training quantization, which is the most widely used approach for efficient model deployment.

weaknesses.value: Inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff alpha 0.623) is moderate, indicating residual subjectivity in safety labels.

ev.quote: The interrater agreement, measured using Krippendorff's α, yielded a score of 0.623.

limitations.value: Tested only on data-centre GPUs (A40, T4); no edge or mobile deployment is evaluated.

ev.quote: Hardware For LLM Inference - 4 x NVIDIA A40 GPUs (48GB VRAM each).

limitations.value: No latency, throughput, or energy measurements; the work treats quantization as a quality study only.

ev.quote: Compute Requirements LLM workflows: ≈ 80 total GPU-hours (A40). AlignScore evaluation: ≈ 40 total GPU-hours (T4)

limitations.value: Mechanistic / interpretability analysis is absent; findings are behavioural, not causal at the layer or feature level.

ev.quote: QUIK retains a small set of full-precision, salient vectors, which helps preserve alignment-critical knowledge

limitations.value: Bit widths capped at W2-W4 weight-only; mixed-precision activation and KV-cache quantization are not explored.

ev.quote: focusing on 4-bit and 2-bit precision for weight-only quantization.

future_work_stated.value: Expand dataset selection criteria beyond high-deflection prompts to enhance diversity.

ev.quote: Expanding the selection criteria in future work could further enhance dataset diversity.

future_work_stated.value: Investigate QAT under the same safety and trustworthiness assessments to compare with PTQ more deeply.

ev.quote: Investigating how models trained with quantization-aware training perform under the same safety and trustworthiness assessments could offer additional insights

future_work_stated.value: Develop alignment-aware QAT strategies to preserve, re-align, or adapt SFT/RLHF safety mechanisms under compression.

ev.quote: Future research should account for the fragility of alignment mechanisms introduced during SFT or RLHF. This behavior is sensitive to quantization and should be preserved, re-aligned, or adapted via alignment-aware QAT strategies.
